patients.summary: Retired administrative assistant with type 2 diabetes on insulin, hypertension, CKD 3b and class II obesity who joins the practice after a post-cholecystectomy wound dehiscence. Over six years she accumulates secondary hyperparathyroidism, severe tricuspid regurgitation, left-knee pseudogout, right HZO, two travel-related left leg DVTs and a repaired paraesophageal hernia.

events.reason: Drainage from abdominal incision after surgery

documents.title: Emergency Department Provider Note
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED.

CC: wound leaking.

HPI: 65 y/o woman, post-op day 10 from an open cholecystectomy done here on 9/25. Since yesterday the lower part of her incision has been leaking pinkish, blood-tinged fluid onto her dressing. No fevers, no chills, no belly pain. Eating and drinking fine. Known type 2 diabetes on insulin and hypertension.

Meds: lisinopril 20 daily, amlodipine 5 daily, furosemide 40 daily, metformin 1000 BID, glargine 18 u qHS, atorvastatin 40 daily, acetaminophen 500 q6h prn.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: vitals stable as charted, afebrile. Incision: edges have come apart over a short segment and a little subcutaneous fat is visible at the base. No bowel, no fascial defect seen or felt. Mild redness of the surrounding skin, not warm. No crepitus. Abdomen otherwise soft, nontender. Hemodynamically appropriate throughout.

Labs: WBC 11.0, Hgb 13.2, glucose 180, CRP 15 (ref <10).

MDM: superficial dehiscence of the skin and fat layer only; fascia intact on exam. No signs of a deep infection. Mildly raised WBC and CRP, nonspecific this soon after surgery.

Plan: wound irrigated and loosely packed with saline-moistened gauze, to close from the bottom up. Visiting nurse referral for daily packing changes. No antibiotics. General surgery clinic in 2-3 weeks, sooner with fever, spreading redness or pus. She states she is changing primary care and will bring this record to her new doctor.

Dx: superficial surgical wound dehiscence.

documents.title: Records from prior primary care office
documents.author: front desk
documents.body:

Contents: visit notes 2016-2020, med list, lab flowsheets, immunization record, colonoscopy report.
- Colonoscopy 3/2018: screening, prep good, cecum reached, no polyps. Next in 10 years.
- Problems carried: type 2 diabetes (on insulin for several years), hypertension, CKD stage 3b, osteoarthritis of both knees, high cholesterol, obesity, reflux.
- Surgical: L knee arthroscopy with debridement ~2010; open cholecystectomy 9/2020.
- Immunizations: flu yearly through 2019; pneumococcal and Tdap dates not found.

Indexed to chart for PCP review.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
New patient. 65F transferring care; her old office is closing its doors. Here also because she's 19 days out from an open gallbladder operation and the bottom of the incision opened up last week (ED 10/5, record reviewed).

Wound: visiting nurse coming daily to repack. Less drainage now, no fever. Pain controlled with acetaminophen.

DM2: dx around 2009, on glargine for years plus metformin. Checks sugars mornings, mostly 120s-160s. No lows she knows of. Eye exam last year, she thinks normal.
HTN: on 3 agents incl. furosemide. Home cuff readings 130s.
Kidneys: told CKD stage 3b a couple of years ago. Was never sent to a kidney doctor.
Knees: both ache, L worse, scope on the left ~10 yrs ago. Acetaminophen as needed. Avoids ibuprofen because of her kidneys.
Reflux: heartburn now and then after big meals, uses nothing for it.

FHx: mother and maternal grandmother with type 2 diabetes. Father and a brother with high BP; father had a heart attack at 68. A maternal uncle was on dialysis.
SHx: retired admin assistant. Quit cigarettes ~2008, about 20 pack-years before that. Wine a glass or two a month. Lives alone, independent.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP and pulse as recorded. BMI ~37. Pleasant, in no distress.
HEENT normal. Neck supple, no JVD. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear.
Abdomen: right subcostal incision healed except a 2 cm open segment at the medial end, pink granulation at the base, packing in place, no pus, no surrounding redness.
Ext: no edema. Feet: skin intact, monofilament normal both feet, pulses 2+.
PHQ-2 negative.

A/P
1. Wound dehiscence, healing by secondary intention. Continue VNA packing; surgery clinic visit already booked.
2. DM2 with CKD: A1c, BMP, urine albumin today. Continue metformin and glargine 18 u.
3. HTN: at goal. Same 3 meds.
4. CKD 3b: labs today; will think about nephrology once I see her numbers.
5. Lipids on atorvastatin 40: panel today.
6. Prevention: colonoscopy 2018 clean. Needs mammogram, pneumococcal, Tdap - will catch up at a wellness visit. Flu shot once the wound settles, next few weeks.

RTC 6-8 weeks.

documents.title: Your recent labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Ms. Hughes, your labs are back. Sugar control (A1c) is in a reasonable place for you. Kidney function is about what your old records show, stage 3b, and there is some protein leaking in the urine, which fits with diabetes affecting the kidneys. Blood counts are normal, and cholesterol is well controlled on atorvastatin. No changes for now. We'll talk more at the next visit.

documents.title: RE: Your recent labs
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Thank you doctor. The nurse says the hole is getting smaller.

documents.title: General Surgery Clinic Letter
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Regional hospital, General Surgery Clinic

Re: Joan Hughes, DOB 9/21/1955
Seen 10/29/2020

Dear colleague,

I saw Ms. Hughes in follow-up 5 weeks after her open cholecystectomy, complicated by a small superficial separation at the medial end of the incision that the ED packed on 10/5. She reports less drainage and no fever.

On exam the open segment is now about 1.5 cm long and shallow, with healthy granulation tissue and no slough. No erythema beyond the edge, no fluctuance. The fascia is intact.

The wound is progressing as expected. Visiting nursing will continue daily packing and then simple dressings once it is too shallow to pack. No antibiotics are needed. I will see her again only if it stalls.

Allergies: no known drug allergies.

Sincerely,
General Surgery

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital, Medicine service
Admitted 11/23/2020, discharged 11/27/2020
PCP: Internal Medicine - Primary Care (copy sent)

Reason for admission: about a week of heavy fatigue, generalized itching and poor appetite. Since her surgery in late September she had been eating and drinking much less while continuing her furosemide and lisinopril.

Key data: creatinine 4.3 and BUN 67 on arrival (her outpatient creatinine runs about 1.5). Course: acute worsening of her known stage 3b chronic kidney disease from poor intake on a diuretic and ACE inhibitor. Treated with IV fluids. Lisinopril, furosemide and metformin held. Nephrology consulted in house. Appetite and itching improved, creatinine down to 2.2 on the morning of discharge.

Discharge medications: amlodipine 5 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily (resume), insulin glargine 18 units at bedtime, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, acetaminophen as needed.
HOLD lisinopril and furosemide until seen by PCP with repeat labs.

Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: PCP within 1 week with BMP. Nephrology clinic in about 3 weeks.
Discharge diagnosis: acute on chronic kidney disease stage 3b; type 2 diabetes; hypertension.

documents.title: Post-Discharge Call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called pt after discharge 11/27. Feels much better, eating again, itching mostly gone. Drinking fluids. Not taking lisinopril or furosemide per hospital. Mild ankle puffiness by evening, no SOB. Fasting sugars 140-170. Confirmed appt Wed 12/2 with BMP same day. Pt verbalized understanding.

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth every morning

documents.title: Post-Hospital Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen after her 11/23-11/27 admission for acute on chronic kidney injury (creatinine 4.3, BUN 67 on arrival, 2.2 at discharge). Discharge summary reviewed. She felt wiped out and itchy for a week before going in; looking back, she was barely eating after the gallbladder surgery but kept taking her water pill.

Now: energy better but not back to normal, still a little itchy at night. Eating normally. Off lisinopril and furosemide since admission. Some evening ankle swelling.

Exam: BP as charted. Looks well. Heart RRR. Lungs clear. Trace ankle edema. Incision fully closed, thin pink scar at the medial end.

BMP drawn before the visit: creatinine back to her usual ~1.5, potassium normal.

A/P
1. AKI on CKD 3b, recovered to baseline. Restart lisinopril 20 and furosemide 40. Talked through sick-day rules: if she can't eat or drink, hold the furosemide and lisinopril and call. BMP again in 2 wks with nephrology.
2. Wound dehiscence - healed. Closing this out.
3. DM2: sugars fine, same regimen.
4. Itching/fatigue: watching, nephrology visit 12/21.

RTC 2-3 months.

medications.sig: Take 1 capsule (2,000 units) by mouth daily

documents.title: Nephrology Clinic Letter
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
Outside Nephrology Group

Re: Joan Hughes, 65 y/o F
Visit 12/21/2020

Thank you for sharing her care. I met Ms. Hughes in hospital last month and saw her today in the office.

She was admitted in late November with uremic symptoms; creatinine was 4.3 with a BUN of 67 at that time, from volume depletion on diuretic and ACE inhibitor after surgery. She is better but still tired, and she still itches, mostly at night.

Medications: lisinopril 20 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, furosemide 40 mg, metformin 1000 mg BID, insulin glargine 18 units qHS, atorvastatin 40 mg, acetaminophen prn. Allergies: none known.

Examination: BP 134/76, pulse 80. Unremarkable exam; no edema today, no asterixis, no rub.

Today's labs: creatinine at her baseline (CKD 3b), calcium 9.0, phosphorus 4.4, intact PTH 148 pg/mL, 25-OH vitamin D 21 ng/mL.

Impression
1. CKD stage 3b, diabetic and hypertensive, recovered from the November acute insult.
2. Secondary hyperparathyroidism of renal origin, with low vitamin D contributing.
3. Pruritus and fatigue, likely the tail of the acute episode; should keep improving.

Plan: cholecalciferol 2,000 units daily. Repeat PTH and vitamin D with her yearly labs here. Avoid NSAIDs and keep up the sick-day rules her PCP reviewed. I would like to see her yearly, sooner if her creatinine drifts.

Nephrology

events.reason: Fatigue, leg swelling and shortness of breath

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Over the past several months, slowly worsening tiredness and swelling of both ankles. Now gets winded with very little effort; a single flight of stairs means stopping halfway. No chest pain. Sleeps on one pillow. No cough. She had assumed it was left over from November.

O: BP as charted. No distress at rest. Neck veins look full sitting up. Heart regular with a systolic murmur along the lower left sternal edge I did not hear in October. Lungs clear. 2+ pitting edema both legs to mid-shin.

Labs today: creatinine at baseline, K normal, Hgb normal, A1c pending.

A/P
Exertional dyspnea, bilateral edema, new murmur with full neck veins - right-sided process vs other valve disease. Referred to cardiology, asked them for an echo. Kidney numbers are stable so this isn't the CKD. Continue furosemide 40, keep salt down. If breathing worsens or any chest pain, call or go to ED.
F/u after cardiology.

documents.title: Cardiology Consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside Cardiology Group - Consultation

Re: Joan Hughes, DOB 9/21/1955
Date of visit: 3/23/2021
Referred by: primary care, for breathlessness, edema and a murmur.

History: a few months of progressive breathlessness with minimal exertion; she now struggles with one flight of stairs. Fatigue and swelling in both legs over the same period. Seen by nephrology recently for CKD after a November admission. Medications include lisinopril, furosemide and metformin (full list per PCP). No known drug allergies.

Exam: T 37.0 C, BP 130/80, HR 88, RR 18. Jugular venous pressure up to the angle of the jaw. The liver edge is palpable and pulsatile. 2+ pitting edema to the shins bilaterally. Holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. Lungs clear.

ECG: right axis deviation and right bundle branch block.
Echo today: severe tricuspid regurgitation, dilated RA and RV, RV function mildly reduced, RVSP estimated 38 mmHg, LVEF 60%, no other significant valve lesion.

Assessment: symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation with right-sided congestion; left heart normal.

Plan: sodium under 2 g per day and daily morning weights, call if up 2 kg in a week. Continue furosemide 40 mg daily for now, given her kidney history I prefer not to push the diuretic harder. Not a candidate for valve intervention at this stage. Repeat echo in about a year, sooner with change. Follow up here yearly.

Cardiology

documents.title: salt
documents.author: patient
documents.body: The heart doctor said under 2 grams of salt. Does that count the canned soup? I eat a lot of soup. Also do I weigh myself before or after breakfast

documents.title: RE: salt
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Good questions. Yes, canned soup counts and most cans run 800-1,000 mg sodium each, so look for low-sodium versions or make your own. Weigh first thing in the morning after using the bathroom, before breakfast, same scale each day. Write it down and bring the log to your next visit. Our dietitian handout is attached.

conditions.label: Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis), left knee

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth once daily for 7 days

results.text: Rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals (calcium pyrophosphate)

reports.text: Left knee, three views. Linear calcification within the menisci and articular cartilage (chondrocalcinosis). Joint effusion. No fracture or dislocation. Joint spaces relatively preserved for age.

documents.title: Emergency Department Provider Note
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED, Sunday.

66F with knee OA (L scope ~2010), DM2 on insulin, CKD 3b. Two days ago her left knee became very painful out of nowhere and has gotten steadily worse - now red, hot, swollen, she can barely bend it. No fall, no twist, no injury. No fevers at home.

Meds per pt list. NKDA.

Exam: T 37.2. L knee warm, red, tense effusion, ROM limited by pain to about 30 degrees. R knee cool with crepitus only. No skin break.

Arthrocentesis L knee, sterile prep, lateral approach: 35 mL yellow cloudy fluid. WBC 18,000, 75% PMNs. Polarized microscopy: rhomboid weakly positive birefringent crystals. Gram stain no organisms. Culture sent.
XR: chondrocalcinosis, effusion.

Impression: acute CPPD (pseudogout) flare of the L knee. Gram stain negative; septic joint felt unlikely but culture pending.

Plan: NSAIDs avoided with her kidneys. Colchicine 0.6 mg once daily x 7 days (renal dosing). Ice, rest, acetaminophen. Will call if culture grows. PCP follow-up this week; return for fever or worsening.

documents.title: Call re: ED visit

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP

ED f/u for L knee pseudogout (Sunday). ED note and fluid results reviewed: CPP crystals, Gram stain neg. Culture finalized yesterday, no growth.

Knee much better, maybe 70% - walking with a cane around the house. Day 4 of colchicine, a little loose stool, no diarrhea.

Exam: afebrile. L knee mild warmth, small effusion, flexes to ~90. R knee baseline.

A/P: acute CPPD flare, improving. Finish 7 days of colchicine, stop sooner if diarrhea. Back to acetaminophen. Told her the crystals can flare again in the same joint; if so call early. Sugars ran a bit high in the ED, fine now.

reports.text: Compared with 3/2021. LV normal size and function, LVEF 55-60%. RV remains dilated with mildly reduced function. RA dilated. Severe tricuspid regurgitation, unchanged. Estimated RVSP 38 mmHg. Other valves without significant disease. No effusion.

documents.title: Phone Call with PCP

Pt called first thing. Since about Wednesday a burning, stinging pain on the R side of her forehead; yesterday blisters came up over the forehead and around the R eye, and this morning the eye is red, watery and blurry. documents.title: Ophthalmology Consultation
documents.author: ophthalmology
documents.body:
Outside Ophthalmology Practice

Re: Joan Hughes, 67 y/o, seen 3/27/2023 at the request of her PCP.

History: burning pain over the right forehead starting 5 days ago, followed by a blistering rash. No similar episode before, no recent illness or injury. Diabetes and hypertension controlled. Takes metformin and lisinopril among others; NKDA.

Exam: vesicular eruption confined to the right V1 dermatome (forehead, upper lid). Visual acuity 20/60 OD, 20/25 OS. Right conjunctiva injected. Fluorescein: dendriform epithelial lesions of the right cornea. Anterior chamber quiet. Left eye normal.

Assessment: herpes zoster ophthalmicus, right, with epithelial keratitis.

Plan: valacyclovir 1 g every 12 hours for 7 days (adjusted for her kidney function). Preservative-free artificial tears four times daily. Cool compresses to the skin. Return 1 week, sooner with worse pain or vision.

Ophthalmology

Arrived 4/4/2024 09:40, discharged 4/5/2024 13:15

68F, CKD 3b, DM2, class II obesity, longstanding bilateral ankle swelling from tricuspid regurgitation. Woke today with the left calf suddenly swollen and throbbing, tight, worse to walk on. Landed two days ago from a 12-hour flight home from abroad. No injury. Denies chest pain, breathlessness, coughing blood.

Vitals stable as charted.
Exam: left leg visibly bigger than right, pitting to the knee, calf tender, Homans positive. Rest of exam unremarkable apart from her known murmur.

Labs: PT/INR, aPTT, platelets normal. Creatinine at her stage 3b baseline.
Duplex: acute thrombus L common femoral and proximal femoral veins.

Assessment: acute left iliofemoral DVT, provoked by long-haul travel. No features of PE.

Plan: fondaparinux 7.5 mg SC daily (weight 98 kg; dose acceptable at her CrCl, with monitoring). Kept overnight in observation to teach injections and watch for bleeding - none; pain already easing. Thigh-high compression stockings. Expected treatment course 3 months, PCP to manage. Return for chest pain, shortness of breath, bleeding.

NKDA.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm, rate 98. Right bundle branch block, unchanged from 2021. No acute ST elevation or depression.
reports.conclusion: Sinus rhythm, RBBB, no acute ischemic change.

reports.text: CT angiogram of the chest with IV contrast. No filling defect in the pulmonary arteries. Large paraesophageal hiatal hernia with most of the stomach above the diaphragm, compressing the adjacent left lower lobe. The stomach enhances normally; no organoaxial or mesenteroaxial twist, no wall thickening, pneumatosis or free air. Right heart chambers dilated. No pleural effusion.
reports.conclusion: No pulmonary embolism. Large paraesophageal hiatal hernia with intrathoracic stomach, no volvulus or ischemia.

Regional hospital ED

69F, reflux, prior L leg DVT (2024), severe TR, CKD 3b, DM2. Four hours of abrupt, severe, sharp chest pain with shortness of breath; worse lying back, better leaning forward/sitting up. On questioning, about a year of food sticking now and then and feeling full quickly after meals, which she chalked up to reflux.

BP 150/90, HR 98, RR 22, SpO2 94% RA.
Abdomen soft, nontender. Breath sounds reduced at the L base. Known LLSB murmur.

Labs: Hgb 13.2, WBC 9.0, plt 250, glucose 180, Cr 1.52, ALT 30, AST 28. hs-troponin normal x2. ECG: RBBB, old.
CXR: retrocardiac air-fluid level.
CTA chest: no PE. Large paraesophageal hernia, most of the stomach in the chest, no volvulus or ischemia.

Assessment: symptomatic large paraesophageal hiatal hernia. PE excluded. Surgery consulted, admitting.
Started pantoprazole 40 daily. NKDA.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Regional hospital, General Surgery
Admitted 4/3/2025 via ED, discharged 4/6/2025

Diagnosis: large paraesophageal hiatal hernia, symptomatic, without volvulus or strangulation.

Course: kept NPO initially with IV fluids; insulin glargine reduced while not eating, metformin held. Pain settled within 24 hours. Diet advanced to soft solids, tolerated. Breathing comfortable, SpO2 mid-90s on room air. Creatinine stable.

Given her symptoms and the size of the hernia, we recommend elective laparoscopic repair with fundoplication. She agrees; surgery scheduled for 5/19/2025.

Discharge medications: home medications at prior doses (lisinopril 20, amlodipine 5, furosemide 40, metformin 1000 BID, glargine 18 u, atorvastatin 40, cholecalciferol, acetaminophen prn), plus NEW pantoprazole 40 mg daily.
Diet: small soft meals, upright 2 hours after eating.
Return for recurrent severe chest pain, vomiting, inability to swallow.
NKDA.
General Surgery

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:

No chest pain since discharge. Eating small soft meals, no sticking. Taking pantoprazole. Sugars a little high the first days home, settling.

Exam: BP and SpO2 as charted. Breath sounds slightly reduced L base. Abdomen soft. Murmur as before.

A/P
1. Paraesophageal hiatal hernia - elective lap repair 5/19. Continue pantoprazole, small meals, upright after eating. ED if severe chest pain or can't keep food down.
2. DM2: back on usual regimen. Around surgery follow the surgeon's insulin instructions.
3. Med rec done with her bottles.

Course: clear liquids POD0, full liquids POD1. Pain controlled with acetaminophen. Glucose managed with reduced glargine while on liquids. Ambulating. Sequential compression devices in house given her DVT history.

Discharge: post-fundoplication diet (liquids 1 week, then soft for 3 weeks). Continue pantoprazole 40 mg daily until clinic. Resume home medications; glargine 18 units once eating soft foods.
Clinic in 4-5 weeks.
NKDA.
